ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II-III), severe alcoholic hepatitis on corticosteroids — concurrent moderate alcohol withdrawal (CIWA 12) and hypoglycemia (glucose 62-64) as critical co-precipitants; high Wernicke risk given chronic alcohol and malnutrition.

differential.diagnosis: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome with delirium tremens
differential.key_features: Confusion 48 h post-last drink + tremor + autonomic features fit withdrawal; CIWA 12 = moderate; coexists with HE and requires careful adjunctive treatment (avoid scheduled benzos).
Chronic alcohol + malnutrition + chronic pancreatitis = high thiamine-deficiency risk; thiamine 28 nmol/L low; treat empirically with high-dose IV thiamine regardless of MRI.
Glucose 62-64 contributes to confusion and is itself critical to correct (after thiamine).
Alcoholic hepatitis on steroids is immunosuppressed; screen with blood/urine cultures and paracentesis if ascites.
Prednisolone can cause neuropsychiatric symptoms but does not produce asterixis; consider only if other precipitants are excluded.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering prednisolone, lactulose, rifaximin, any benzodiazepines in use — minimize benzodiazepine exposure; phenobarbital or careful adjuncts preferred for withdrawal; flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Periaqueductal gray and mammillary body T2/FLAIR signal would confirm Wernicke; absent signal does NOT exclude — thiamine given empirically anyway. Required given high Wernicke pre-test probability.

Consult hepatology and critical care; consider transplant evaluation if Lille day-7 indicates non-response — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.
In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect on neuroimaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: High-dose IV thiamine 500 mg TID for 3 days BEFORE any dextrose (Wernicke prophylaxis/treatment) — empirical regardless of MRI.
Correct hypoglycemia AFTER thiamine; maintain euglycemia.
IV magnesium and potassium repletion (Mg 1.4, K 3.0).
Lactulose titrated to 2-4 soft stools/day; rifaximin 550 mg BID.

Treat alcohol withdrawal with symptom-triggered protocol preferring phenobarbital or adjunctive clonidine/gabapentin; use benzodiazepines only at lowest effective doses when essential (e.g., severe agitation, seizures).
Re-assess steroid response on day 7 (Lille score); discontinue prednisolone if non-responder.
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not give dextrose before thiamine in any alcoholic patient — precipitates Wernicke.
Do not use scheduled (fixed-dose) benzodiazepines as withdrawal prophylaxis in this patient; HE precipitation risk outweighs benefit at moderate CIWA.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.

When HE and alcohol withdrawal coexist, the treatment dilemma is real: scheduled benzodiazepines worsen HE while undertreated withdrawal risks seizures. Symptom-triggered, lowest-dose, short-acting agents (lorazepam) are preferred over scheduled long-acting drugs (chlordiazepoxide); phenobarbital is a useful alternative.
Thiamine must be given before any glucose; the 'banana bag' tradition is supported here.
